screens.title: Traffic Shaping, QoS, and Bandwidth Management
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we learn how to make bandwidth predictable and fair on RHEL systems. You will see why simply increasing capacity is not enough and how traffic shaping and Quality of Service let you guarantee critical services get the bandwidth and low latency they require. We focus on the tc command, the building blocks it exposes — root qdisc, classes, filters, and leaves — and two practical qdiscs: the Token Bucket Filter for simple rate limits and Hierarchical Token Bucket for hierarchical prioritization and guarantees. I'll give concrete command examples you can run in a lab, show how to map ports and services to classes, and explain common mistakes that can block traffic if applied incorrectly. By the end you will be able to design a policy, implement HTB classes and u32 filters, and verify behavior with tc statistics and iperf3 tests. Think of this chapter as the toolkit that protects your SSH, VoIP, and replication traffic when networks are congested. Ready to prioritize what matters on your server?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide our work with traffic shaping and QoS on RHEL. First, you will understand the core concepts: what traffic shaping, Quality of Service, and bandwidth management mean in practice and why they are needed when many services share one interface. This conceptual foundation helps you reason about guarantees, ceilings, and latency. Second, you will be able to use the tc command to create queuing disciplines, classes, and filters. That includes practical familiarity with HTB and TBF qdiscs through concrete commands and configuration patterns. Third, you will learn to map services — for example SSH, HTTP, and bulk transfers — to classes, giving each an appropriate guaranteed rate and a maximum ceil. Finally, you will practice verifying and monitoring configurations with iperf3 and tc statistics, and learn how to interpret those counters to confirm traffic is being classified correctly. Each objective links knowledge with a small practical skill so you can both design and validate policies in a controlled environment.

screens.title: What is Traffic Shaping and Why It Matters
screens.narratorSegment: Traffic shaping is the controlled pacing of outbound packets so that the network behaves predictably under contention. In practice this means you intentionally delay or limit transmissions so high-priority services retain responsiveness when many flows compete for the same interface. A clear definition helps: shaping controls the rate at which packets leave an interface; QoS provides mechanisms to prioritize some packets over others; bandwidth management organizes allocation and limits. For example, on a server hosting both nightly backups and interactive SSH sessions, shaping guarantees a minimum for SSH so an administrator can still connect during backups. A common misconception is that setting a rate alone ensures low latency — but without proper priorities and qdisc choice, bursts or misclassification can still starve latency-sensitive traffic. Another useful analogy is plumbing: shaping is a valve that meters flow, HTB is a hierarchy of valves, and TBF is a single valve with a token bucket that refills at a steady pace. When designing a policy, quantify minimums, determine ceilings for bursts, and plan filters to map traffic to classes. The core takeaway is that shaping gives you predictable trade-offs between throughput and latency when capacity alone is insufficient. Consider: which services on your server must remain responsive during heavy transfers?

Core Concept › Traffic Shaping
Controlled pacing of packets
Delay or limit transmissions so critical services keep usable performance under load.
Key points
  • Shaping enforces a long-term rate while allowing configured bursts.
  • QoS assigns priority so latency-sensitive flows go first when contention occurs.
  • Design requires rates, ceilings, and classification rules that map traffic to classes.
Analogy
Think of shaping as plumbing valves: HTB is a network of valves sharing a pipe; TBF is a single valve that refills tokens at a steady rate.
Concrete example
A server sending backups could saturate a 100 Mbps link and block SSH. By assigning SSH a guaranteed 5 Mbps and a higher priority, administrators retain remote access even while bulk transfers use leftover capacity.
Key Takeaway

Shaping balances fairness and responsiveness so critical services remain usable under contention.

screens.title: tc architecture: qdiscs, classes, filters, and leaves
screens.narratorSegment: To work effectively with tc you need to understand its building blocks and how they link. Each network interface has a root qdisc — the entry point that receives all outbound packets. A qdisc can be a simple discipline like TBF, or a tree-based discipline like HTB. Within a tree qdisc you create classes. Classes represent shareable buckets of bandwidth and hold guarantees and ceilings. Leaves are the qdiscs attached to classes that perform the actual scheduling or shaping. Filters inspect packet attributes — ports, IPs, protocols — and assign a packet to a class. For example, you might set a root HTB qdisc, add a parent class for the total 100 Mbps, then child classes for SSH, HTTP, and bulk traffic. Filters using u32 matches bind dport values to those child classes. A common misconception is thinking qdisc equals class; instead qdiscs are algorithms and classes are allocation containers. Visually, imagine a root handle that branches into classids with numeric handles you reference when adding filters. Correct handle and classid values are essential; mismatches in those identifiers or applying rules to the wrong interface are frequent causes of unexpected results. Understanding this architecture makes command sequences and troubleshooting predictable.

keyIdea.title: Architecture insight
keyIdea.text: Root qdisc receives traffic; classes allocate bandwidth; filters map packets to classes; leaves implement the scheduling or rate limit.

content.html:
Definition › tc components
Component map
Root qdisc (handle)
Entry point for all outgoing packets on an interface.
Classes (classid)
Allocation units with rate and ceil values.
Filters
Classification rules that assign packets to classes.
Leaves
Attached qdiscs that implement shaping or scheduling.
Practical notes
  • Always confirm interface name; wrong interface means no effect.
  • Handles and classids must match when you reference them in filters.
  • Leaves perform the actual token bucket or scheduler work for each class.
Common mistake
Forgetting to delete an existing qdisc before adding a new root qdisc can leave unexpected behavior; use tc qdisc del dev eth0 root to clear.

screens.title: Using TBF for simple rate limiting
screens.narratorSegment: The Token Bucket Filter is the go-to qdisc for a single-stream rate limit. Its model is straightforward: tokens accumulate in a bucket at a configured rate. A packet may be sent only if the bucket has enough tokens for its size; otherwise the packet waits until tokens arrive. This makes TBF ideal when you want to ensure outbound traffic never exceeds a sustained rate, but still permit short bursts. The chapter gives a clear example of limiting eth0 to one megabit per second with a small burst and a latency parameter. In a lab you would first clear existing qdiscs, then add a TBF on the root. The latency parameter determines how long packets may be queued before being dropped, which matters for bufferbloat. One misconception is treating TBF like a hierarchical scheduler; it is not — it controls a single channel. Use HTB when you need multiple classes and guaranteed minima. In practice, TBF is useful to constrain egress to an ISP link or to cap a noisy service. Try adjusting burst and latency to see how short spikes are handled differently from sustained load.

keyIdea.title: TBF essence
keyIdea.text: TBF enforces a steady sustained rate with controlled bursts via tokens; use it to cap a single stream's egress bandwidth.

content.html:
Process Flow › TBF rate limit
How TBF works
Tokens are added at the configured rate. Packets consume tokens. If the bucket lacks tokens, packets are delayed until tokens accumulate.
When to use
  • To cap outbound bandwidth for a single class or application.
  • When you do not need hierarchical sharing across multiple services.
  • To prevent an interface from exceeding an ISP limit.
Example command
sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root tbf rate 1mbit burst 10kb latency 70ms
This sets eth0 to 1 megabit sustained, a 10 kilobyte burst allowance, and a queuing latency so packets are not held indefinitely before being dropped.
Key Takeaway
TBF is simple and effective for single-stream rate limits; adjust burst and latency to control short spikes and buffer time.

screens.title: HTB: Hierarchical Token Bucket for prioritization
screens.narratorSegment: HTB is the workhorse when you need to allocate bandwidth among multiple services. It creates a tree of classes where a parent class represents a shared pool and child classes receive guaranteed rates and ceilings. A guaranteed rate is the minimum bandwidth a class can obtain; the ceil is the maximum it may burst to when spare bandwidth is available. Priorities affect which classes draw their guarantees first when there is contention. A typical deployment on a 100 Mbps interface uses a parent class for the full link and child classes for SSH, HTTP, and bulk traffic with different rates and ceilings. Filters using u32 matches assign traffic into those child classes by matching destination ports. A common error is assigning incorrect prio values so bulk transfers steal resources from latency-sensitive classes even when rates are set. Testing with tc -s class show reveals usage counters and helps you adjust prio, rate, and ceil. HTB is flexible: use it when you need both guarantees and controlled sharing across multiple traffic types. HTB: Hierarchical Token Bucket for prioritization means htb lets you set guaranteed minima and maximum ceilings in a hierarchy, enabling both guarantees and fair sharing of spare capacity.. In practical terms, create parent and child classes to guarantee rates and allow bursts up to a ceil. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › HTB hierarchy
Parent and child classes
Create a parent for the total bandwidth, then child classes for services with rate, ceil, and priority attributes.
Example attributes
  • rate: guaranteed minimum bandwidth.
  • ceil: maximum burstable bandwidth.
  • prio: numerical preference used during contention.
Commands (pattern)
sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root handle 1: htb default 30
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:1 htb rate 100mbit ceil 100mbit
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1:1 classid 1:10 htb rate 5mbit ceil 20mbit prio 1
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1:1 classid 1:20 htb rate 10mbit ceil 50mbit prio 2
These commands form a parent class and two children with different guarantees and ceilings.

screens.title: Classifying traffic with filters
screens.narratorSegment: Filters are the mechanism that connects observed packets to the classes you created. The u32 filter lets you match packet header fields such as destination port, protocol, or IP address and direct that traffic to a target class. For instance, matching destination port 22 will send SSH packets to a high-priority class. Filters have priorities themselves, and a catch-all filter may be required to place remaining traffic into a default class. A typical sequence uses three filters: SSH to class 1:10, HTTP/HTTPS to class 1:20, and a catch-all to the default class. A common mistake is relying on default values without verifying which class id the root default maps to; confirm your default mapping or explicitly add a catch-all filter. When filters are applied, validate with tc filter show and then watch class byte counters with tc -s class show to ensure traffic hits the expected target. In practice, updating filters lets you change classification rules without rebuilding the entire HTB tree, which is handy during iterative tuning. Classifying traffic with filters means u32 filters match packet fields and assign flows to classes; verify matches using tc filter show and class counters.. In practical terms, use u32 filters to match ports and map flows to htb classes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: u32 filters match packet fields and assign flows to classes; verify matches using tc filter show and class counters.

content.html:
Process Flow › Filters & Classification
Filter patterns
Use u32 to match ports and assign flowid to a class. Filters can be prioritized so exact matches are evaluated first.
Verification
  • tc filter show dev eth0 to list filters.
  • tc -s class show dev eth0 to view counters for each class.
Typical filter commands
sudo tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent 1:0 prio 1 u32 match ip dport 22 0xffff flowid 1:10
sudo tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent 1:0 prio 2 u32 match ip dport 80 0xffff flowid 1:20
sudo tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent 1:0 prio 99 u32 match ip dst 0.0.0.0/0 flowid 1:30
The catch-all ensures unclassified traffic goes to the default child class.

screens.title: Designing a traffic shaping policy
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a traffic shaping policy is a structured process. Start by listing critical services and their performance requirements: which need low latency, which require throughput guarantees, and which are bulk background transfers. Next quantify minimum and maximum bandwidth for each service — a guaranteed rate and a ceil. With those numbers, choose the qdisc: HTB for multiple services with hierarchical guarantees, TBF for single-stream rate limiting. Create a parent class representing total available bandwidth and child classes for each service with rate, ceil, and prio settings. Then write filters that reliably map traffic to classes; match by destination ports or addresses. Always include a catch-all class for unclassified traffic to avoid accidentally dropping flows. Test the policy in a controlled lab using iperf3 to generate traffic for each service, and use tc -s outputs to observe counters and verify traffic is hitting expected classes. Finally, iterate: adjust prio or ceil values if a latency-sensitive class is still experiencing jitter. The process discipline — measure, configure, verify, and adjust — is what ensures shaping delivers predictable results in real deployments. Designing a traffic shaping policy means a repeatable design process: identify, quantify, choose qdisc, implement classes/filters, test, and iterate using tc stats and iperf3.. In practical terms, identify services, quantify needs, choose qdisc, and implement classes and filters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow › Policy design
Step-by-step
  1. Identify critical services and their latency or throughput needs.
  2. Define guaranteed rate and a reasonable ceil for bursts.
  3. Choose HTB for multi-class hierarchies or TBF for single-stream caps.
  4. Create parent and child classes, then add u32 filters to classify traffic.
  5. Verify with tc -s and iperf3 and iterate until metrics meet requirements.
Scenario snippet
For a 100 Mbps link: reserve 5 Mbps for SSH, 10 Mbps for web, and cap others at 30 Mbps, with ceilings that allow bursts when spare capacity exists.

Important practical notes: replace eth0 with your actual interface and keep a management path in case rules interrupt remote access. Hands-on Activity › Starter HTB
Starter commands (apply in order)
sudo tc qdisc del dev eth0 root 2>/dev/null
sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root handle 1: htb default 30
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:1 htb rate 100mbit ceil 100mbit
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1:1 classid 1:10 htb rate 5mbit ceil 20mbit prio 1
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1:1 classid 1:20 htb rate 10mbit ceil 50mbit prio 2
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1:1 classid 1:30 htb rate 1kbit ceil 30mbit prio 3
sudo tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent 1:0 prio 1 u32 match ip dport 22 0xffff flowid 1:10
sudo tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent 1:0 prio 2 u32 match ip dport 80 0xffff flowid 1:20
sudo tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent 1:0 prio 2 u32 match ip dport 443 0xffff flowid 1:20
sudo tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent 1:0 prio 99 u32 match ip dst 0.0.0.0/0 flowid 1:30
Replace eth0 with your interface and run these in a controlled lab. Verify with tc qdisc show and tc -s class show.
Example scenario
SSH needs a guaranteed small bandwidth; HTTP can burst when unused capacity exists; other traffic is limited to avoid saturating the link.

screens.title: TBF vs HTB — choose the right qdisc
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between TBF and HTB depends on whether you need a single sustained cap or a multi-class hierarchy. TBF is simple and efficient: it limits a single stream to a defined rate with a token bucket that allows short bursts. It is ideal when you want a single outbound cap, for example to ensure a host never exceeds an ISP limit. HTB is more powerful: it creates a parent class with child classes, each with a guaranteed rate and a ceil for bursts, and supports priorities across classes. Use HTB when multiple application types share a single link and you need to guarantee minima while allowing unused capacity to be borrowed. A common misconception is to pick TBF because commands are shorter; in multi-service servers you quickly need HTB to prevent lower-priority bulk transfers from affecting latency-sensitive traffic. Another practical consideration is complexity and verification: HTB configurations require careful handle and classid management and more verification steps using tc -s class show. In short: TBF for simple caps, HTB for multi-service prioritization and sharing. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Comparison › TBF vs HTB
TBF

screens.title: Troubleshooting tc configurations and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting tc configurations depends on using the right diagnostic commands and knowing common failure modes. Use tc qdisc show dev eth0 to check the qdisc tree and handles. Use tc -s qdisc show dev eth0 and tc -s class show dev eth0 to obtain statistics such as packet and byte counters; these show whether traffic is actually hitting the expected qdisc or class. Use tc filter show dev eth0 to inspect filters and validate matching criteria. Frequent mistakes include wrong handle or classid values, typos in port numbers or IP addresses in u32 matches, and applying rules to the wrong interface. Another serious problem is forgetting to clear an existing qdisc before adding a new root, which can leave hidden disciplines active. Misconfigured priorities can let bulk traffic consume bandwidth that should be reserved for latency-sensitive flows. If VoIP shows jitter despite a rate setting, verify prio values and check the bytes counters to see which class actually carried the traffic. Always test changes in a controlled environment and keep an out-of-band login method available in case management access is disrupted by a rule change.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we learn how to make bandwidth predictable and fair on RHEL systems. You will see why simply increasing capacity is not enough and how traffic shaping and Quality of Service let you guarantee critical services get the bandwidth and low latency they require. We focus on the tc command, the building blocks it exposes — root qdisc, classes, filters, and leaves — and two practical qdiscs: the Token Bucket Filter for simple rate limits and Hierarchical Token Bucket for hierarchical prioritization and guarantees. I'll give concrete command examples you can run in a lab, show how to map ports and services to classes, and explain common mistakes that can block traffic if applied incorrectly. By the end you will be able to design a policy, implement HTB classes and u32 filters, and verify behavior with tc statistics and iperf3 tests. Think of this chapter as the toolkit that protects your SSH, VoIP, and replication traffic when networks are congested. Ready to prioritize what matters on your server?

These objectives guide our work with traffic shaping and QoS on RHEL. First, you will understand the core concepts: what traffic shaping, Quality of Service, and bandwidth management mean in practice and why they are needed when many services share one interface. This conceptual foundation helps you reason about guarantees, ceilings, and latency. Second, you will be able to use the tc command to create queuing disciplines, classes, and filters. That includes practical familiarity with HTB and TBF qdiscs through concrete commands and configuration patterns. Third, you will learn to map services — for example SSH, HTTP, and bulk transfers — to classes, giving each an appropriate guaranteed rate and a maximum ceil. Finally, you will practice verifying and monitoring configurations with iperf3 and tc statistics, and learn how to interpret those counters to confirm traffic is being classified correctly. Each objective links knowledge with a small practical skill so you can both design and validate policies in a controlled environment.

This second objectives slide focuses on implementation and troubleshooting. You will learn to design a traffic shaping policy: identify critical services, quantify minimum and burst bandwidth, and choose an appropriate qdisc. The chapter supplies hands-on commands to create an HTB tree and to add u32 filters to map traffic to classes. You will also learn TBF for simple rate limiting where a single sustained cap is required. A crucial skill is verifying your applied rules: reading tc qdisc and class statistics to see packet and byte counters and making adjustments when a class is not behaving as expected. Finally, we practice safe deployment techniques: clear existing qdiscs before applying new ones and keep an out-of-band access method in case rules accidentally block management traffic. These skills combine design thinking, exact command usage, and verification so you can deploy shaping safely in production or a controlled lab.

Traffic shaping is the controlled pacing of outbound packets so that the network behaves predictably under contention. In practice this means you intentionally delay or limit transmissions so high-priority services retain responsiveness when many flows compete for the same interface. A clear definition helps: shaping controls the rate at which packets leave an interface; QoS provides mechanisms to prioritize some packets over others; bandwidth management organizes allocation and limits. For example, on a server hosting both nightly backups and interactive SSH sessions, shaping guarantees a minimum for SSH so an administrator can still connect during backups. A common misconception is that setting a rate alone ensures low latency — but without proper priorities and qdisc choice, bursts or misclassification can still starve latency-sensitive traffic. Another useful analogy is plumbing: shaping is a valve that meters flow, HTB is a hierarchy of valves, and TBF is a single valve with a token bucket that refills at a steady pace. When designing a policy, quantify minimums, determine ceilings for bursts, and plan filters to map traffic to classes. The core takeaway is that shaping gives you predictable trade-offs between throughput and latency when capacity alone is insufficient. Consider: which services on your server must remain responsive during heavy transfers?

To work effectively with tc you need to understand its building blocks and how they link. Each network interface has a root qdisc — the entry point that receives all outbound packets. A qdisc can be a simple discipline like TBF, or a tree-based discipline like HTB. Within a tree qdisc you create classes. Classes represent shareable buckets of bandwidth and hold guarantees and ceilings. Leaves are the qdiscs attached to classes that perform the actual scheduling or shaping. Filters inspect packet attributes — ports, IPs, protocols — and assign a packet to a class. For example, you might set a root HTB qdisc, add a parent class for the total 100 Mbps, then child classes for SSH, HTTP, and bulk traffic. Filters using u32 matches bind dport values to those child classes. A common misconception is thinking qdisc equals class; instead qdiscs are algorithms and classes are allocation containers. Visually, imagine a root handle that branches into classids with numeric handles you reference when adding filters. Correct handle and classid values are essential; mismatches in those identifiers or applying rules to the wrong interface are frequent causes of unexpected results. Understanding this architecture makes command sequences and troubleshooting predictable.

The Token Bucket Filter is the go-to qdisc for a single-stream rate limit. Its model is straightforward: tokens accumulate in a bucket at a configured rate. A packet may be sent only if the bucket has enough tokens for its size; otherwise the packet waits until tokens arrive. This makes TBF ideal when you want to ensure outbound traffic never exceeds a sustained rate, but still permit short bursts. The chapter gives a clear example of limiting eth0 to one megabit per second with a small burst and a latency parameter. In a lab you would first clear existing qdiscs, then add a TBF on the root. The latency parameter determines how long packets may be queued before being dropped, which matters for bufferbloat. One misconception is treating TBF like a hierarchical scheduler; it is not — it controls a single channel. Use HTB when you need multiple classes and guaranteed minima. In practice, TBF is useful to constrain egress to an ISP link or to cap a noisy service. Try adjusting burst and latency to see how short spikes are handled differently from sustained load.

HTB is the workhorse when you need to allocate bandwidth among multiple services. It creates a tree of classes where a parent class represents a shared pool and child classes receive guaranteed rates and ceilings. A guaranteed rate is the minimum bandwidth a class can obtain; the ceil is the maximum it may burst to when spare bandwidth is available. Priorities affect which classes draw their guarantees first when there is contention. A typical deployment on a 100 Mbps interface uses a parent class for the full link and child classes for SSH, HTTP, and bulk traffic with different rates and ceilings. Filters using u32 matches assign traffic into those child classes by matching destination ports. A common error is assigning incorrect prio values so bulk transfers steal resources from latency-sensitive classes even when rates are set. Testing with tc -s class show reveals usage counters and helps you adjust prio, rate, and ceil. HTB is flexible: use it when you need both guarantees and controlled sharing across multiple traffic types. HTB: Hierarchical Token Bucket for prioritization means htb lets you set guaranteed minima and maximum ceilings in a hierarchy, enabling both guarantees and fair sharing of spare capacity.. In practical terms, create parent and child classes to guarantee rates and allow bursts up to a ceil. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Filters are the mechanism that connects observed packets to the classes you created. The u32 filter lets you match packet header fields such as destination port, protocol, or IP address and direct that traffic to a target class. For instance, matching destination port 22 will send SSH packets to a high-priority class. Filters have priorities themselves, and a catch-all filter may be required to place remaining traffic into a default class. A typical sequence uses three filters: SSH to class 1:10, HTTP/HTTPS to class 1:20, and a catch-all to the default class. A common mistake is relying on default values without verifying which class id the root default maps to; confirm your default mapping or explicitly add a catch-all filter. When filters are applied, validate with tc filter show and then watch class byte counters with tc -s class show to ensure traffic hits the expected target. In practice, updating filters lets you change classification rules without rebuilding the entire HTB tree, which is handy during iterative tuning. Classifying traffic with filters means u32 filters match packet fields and assign flows to classes; verify matches using tc filter show and class counters.. In practical terms, use u32 filters to match ports and map flows to htb classes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Designing a traffic shaping policy is a structured process. Start by listing critical services and their performance requirements: which need low latency, which require throughput guarantees, and which are bulk background transfers. Next quantify minimum and maximum bandwidth for each service — a guaranteed rate and a ceil. With those numbers, choose the qdisc: HTB for multiple services with hierarchical guarantees, TBF for single-stream rate limiting. Create a parent class representing total available bandwidth and child classes for each service with rate, ceil, and prio settings. Then write filters that reliably map traffic to classes; match by destination ports or addresses. Always include a catch-all class for unclassified traffic to avoid accidentally dropping flows. Test the policy in a controlled lab using iperf3 to generate traffic for each service, and use tc -s outputs to observe counters and verify traffic is hitting expected classes. Finally, iterate: adjust prio or ceil values if a latency-sensitive class is still experiencing jitter. The process discipline — measure, configure, verify, and adjust — is what ensures shaping delivers predictable results in real deployments. Designing a traffic shaping policy means a repeatable design process: identify, quantify, choose qdisc, implement classes/filters, test, and iterate using tc stats and iperf3..
